biography: A priest of Ripon and member of Bishop Wilfrid's household, conventionally identified with the Æddi Stephanus whom Bede says Wilfrid brought back from Kent as a singing-master (fl. c. 670-720). He accompanied Wilfrid on his journeys and wrote the Vita Sancti Wilfridi (c. 712-714) at the request of Acca of Hexham and Tatberht of Ripon. Nothing else is known of his life, and even his identification with Bede's 'Æddi' rests on a plausible but unproven equation.
literary_profile: The earliest identifiable Anglo-Latin biographer after the anonymous Lindisfarne life of Cuthbert. His Vita Wilfridi is a partisan defence of his hero against the charges of Wilfrid's enemies, cast in the conventions of late-antique hagiography.
stylistic_characteristics: Vigorous, episodic narrative with a strong authorial voice; vivid set-piece scenes (Wilfrid's shipwreck, his Roman appeals, his deathbed); simpler and more direct Latin than Aldhelm's, with a notable absence of the hermeneutic manner.
intellectual_concerns: Episcopal authority and the primacy of Rome; the sanctity of a controversial political bishop; the deeds of the apostolic missionary as evidence of holiness.
historical_significance: His Vita Wilfridi is the earliest surviving biography written in England about a contemporary English churchman, and a principal source for the history of the seventh-century Northumbrian church and Wilfrid's career.
major_influences: The anonymous Life of St Cuthbert (Lindisfarne)
biographical_uncertainty: Identification with Bede's Æddi Stephanus is traditional, not proven. Birth and death dates unknown; floruit c. 670-720.

literary_identity: monastic reformer; Latin and Old English prose writer; translator
biography: Born into a noble Winchester family c. 904-909, brought up at the court of King Æthelstan, and ordained with Dunstan. He became a monk at Glastonbury under Dunstan, was made abbot of the derelict monastery of Abingdon (c. 954), and in 963 was appointed bishop of Winchester, where he expelled the secular clerics of the Old and New Minsters and installed monks. He was the most radical and effective leader of the Benedictine Reform, a teacher of Ælfric, and a patron of manuscript production and the arts. He died on 1 August 984.
literary_profile: Author of the Regularis Concordia (c. 970), the customary that unified English monastic observance under royal patronage; traditionally credited with the Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict (c. 960s) and associated with the Old English New Minster Charter (966) and possibly the Benedictine Office. His school at Winchester created the standardized literary language ('Winchester words') used by Ælfric.
stylistic_characteristics: In the Regularis Concordia, clear expository Latin organized for practical liturgical use, with vivid prescriptions for ceremony (the Visitatio Sepulchri, the 'tropes'); in the vernacular Rule, plain idiomatic Old English translating Benedict's Latin closely.
intellectual_concerns: Uniformity of observance; the king as protector of reformed monasticism; the education of monks in Latin and the vernacular; the liturgy as the centre of the religious life.
historical_significance: The architect of the English Benedictine Reform and of the alliance between the crown and the reformed monasteries; his Winchester school and standardized Old English shaped the literary language of the late tenth century and of Ælfric's and Wulfstan's prose.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth year approximate (c. 904-909). The attribution of the Old English Benedictine Rule and Benedictine Office to him is traditional and widely but not universally accepted.

literary_identity: hagiographer, grammarian, computist; Latin prose writer
biography: Born c. 945 near Orléans, oblate of Fleury, and trained there in grammar, dialectic, and computus. At the invitation of Oswald of Worcester he taught at Ramsey Abbey in the Fenland from 985 to 987, where he wrote the Passio Sancti Eadmundi at the request of the Ramsey monks and dedicated it to Dunstan. Returning to Fleury, he became abbot in 988 and defended his monastery against episcopal encroachment; he died in 1004 in a brawl at La Réole while attempting to reform the priory of La Réole.
literary_profile: One of the leading scholars of tenth-century Europe. At Ramsey he composed the Passio Sancti Eadmundi (985-987), the earliest Latin life of King Edmund of East Anglia and the basis of Ælfric's Old English life; his other works include the Quaestiones grammaticales (dedicated to his English students), computistical treatises, and the Collectio canonum.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, correct Latin prose with the polish of the Fleury school; the Passio builds its narrative through dramatic dialogue and carefully staged scenes of Edmund's martyrdom and the discovery of his incorrupt body.
intellectual_concerns: The union of grammar, computus, and exegesis in monastic learning; royal sanctity and the cult of St Edmund; the reform of monastic discipline.
historical_significance: The principal conduit of continental monastic learning into the English Benedictine Reform; his teaching at Ramsey raised the standard of Latin scholarship in England, and his Passio Eadmundi founded the literary cult of St Edmund, patron saint of the English kingdom.
biographical_uncertainty: None significant for the works recorded here; the Passio's dedication to Dunstan and composition at Ramsey (985-987) are established.

biography: A pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham who identifies himself by the nickname 'Bata' and addresses his master with affectionate humour in the colloquies. He probably taught at a monastic school in the first quarter of the eleventh century (fl. c. 1005-1025). His life is otherwise unknown.
literary_profile: Author of the Colloquia and the Colloquia difficiliora, Latin conversation manuals modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy but far more expansive and boisterous: they dramatize daily life in the monastic school with dialogue about food, drink, beatings, and petty theft.
stylistic_characteristics: Colloquial, hyperbolic Latin with a taste for comic exaggeration and insult; the texts deliberately enlarge the vocabulary of daily life beyond the classroom classics.
intellectual_concerns: The teaching of spoken Latin; the discipline and everyday realities of the monastic school; the relationship between master and pupil.
historical_significance: His colloquies preserve a uniquely vivid picture of eleventh-century English school life and document the vitality of the vernacular-Latin classroom tradition founded by Ælfric.
biographical_uncertainty: Known only from his texts; floruit approximate (c. 1005-1025); birth and death dates unknown.

biography: A Mercian by birth who became a monk at Breedon-on-the-Hill in Leicestershire, a house with Northumbrian connections. He was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in 731, succeeding Berhtwald, and died in office in 734. Bede records his consecration in the Historia ecclesiastica.
literary_profile: Author of the Aenigmata, forty Latin riddles with a preface, on theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects, and of a Latin grammar (Ars Tatuini) based on Donatus. His riddles are the first Latin riddle collection composed in England to survive complete.
stylistic_characteristics: Compact hexameter riddles in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm, but with doctrine rather than natural history as their usual subject; the verse is plain and schoolmasterly rather than hermeneutic.
intellectual_concerns: The union of grammatical learning with theology; the encyclopedic description of creation through the riddle form; Christian teaching for the schoolroom.
historical_significance: With Aldhelm and Hwætberht he established the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that fed into the vernacular Exeter Book Riddles; his grammar helped transmit the Insular grammatical tradition.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and place uncertain (Mercia by tradition); the attribution of the riddles and grammar to him is secure.

biography: A monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow from boyhood who studied in Ireland in his youth and took the religious name Eusebius. He succeeded Ceolfrith as abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow c. 716 and remained abbot until his death c. 747. He was a friend and correspondent of Boniface and a close associate of Bede, who dedicated works to him.
literary_profile: Author of the Aenigmata Eusebii, forty Latin riddles on encyclopedic subjects ranging from the alphabet and the liberal arts to the natural world, composed in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
stylistic_characteristics: Hexameter riddles marked by learned wordplay and allusive density, modelled closely on Aldhelm; the subjects move from grammatical abstraction to cosmology and natural history.
intellectual_concerns: The encyclopedic ordering of knowledge; the riddling description of creation; the transmission of Aldhelmian learning in Northumbria.
historical_significance: His riddles, together with Tatwine's, carried the Aldhelmian riddle tradition into the Northumbrian Renaissance and stand behind the vernacular riddle collection of the Exeter Book.
biographical_uncertainty: Death date approximate (c. 747); the riddles are securely attributed by manuscript tradition.

literary_identity: exegete, canonist, and teacher; Latin prose writer
biography: Born in Tarsus in 602 and educated in the Greek East (probably at Antioch and Constantinople), he was living as a monk in Rome when Pope Vitalian consecrated him archbishop of Canterbury in 668, with Hadrian the African as his companion and adviser. Together they toured England, reformed the English church, and founded the school of Canterbury, where Greek and Latin learning, canon law, and biblical exegesis were taught. He died on 19 September 690.
literary_profile: The Laterculus Malalianus, a Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, is attributed to him (written at Canterbury in the 670s); the biblical commentaries from the Canterbury school preserve his and Hadrian's teaching; the penitential that circulates under his name is traditionally attributed to him. His school produced Aldhelm and the earliest English manuscript culture.
stylistic_characteristics: In the Laterculus Malalianus, dense and sometimes idiosyncratic Latin shaped by Syriac and Greek exegetical sources, with a chronological apparatus; the Canterbury commentaries preserve an unusual blend of Greek and Latin patristic learning.
intellectual_concerns: The chronology and exegesis of the life of Christ; the union of Greek and Latin Christian learning; church order and penance; the education of an English clergy.
historical_significance: As organizer of the Canterbury school he is the founder of Anglo-Saxon Latin learning; his church reforms and synods (Hertford 672, Hatfield 679) unified the English church, and his teaching reached Bede's Northumbria through his pupils.
biographical_uncertainty: The attribution of the Laterculus Malalianus and the Penitential to him is traditional and widely accepted, but not beyond dispute. Birth and death dates are recorded by Bede.
